body.text: In the run-up to the 2026 APEC Summit, the streets of Shenzhen is awash in pink. Bougainvillea, the city’s official flower, is in its annual fall bloom – and this year it has been joined by hundreds of welcoming floral displays and green sculptures. The city is hosting thousands of international visitors for the Economic Leaders’ Meeting on November 18 and 19 – among them U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, who will join Chinese President Xi Jinping for a much anticipated trilateral meeting on November 19.

But beneath the greenery lies a much larger project years in the making. Beijing is in the process of bringing together the Pearl River Delta, a manufacturing belt spanning nine mainland cities, along with Hong Kong and Macao, into an interconnected “megapolis” called the Greater Bay Area (GBA). Hosting international visitors in Shenzhen gives Beijing a stage to showcase both the region’s triumphs and its ambitions for China’s next phase of growth.

With its vibrant manufacturing industry and ports, the Pearl River Delta has long been known as “the world’s factory.” Following China’s reform and opening up, Shenzhen became one of the country’s first Special Economic Zones in 1980, attracting bounds of foreign investors and manufacturers looking to take advantage of cheaper land and labor. Over the decades, garment and toy workshops have gradually given way to sophisticated electronics plants, turning Shenzhen and neighboring Dongguan into major hubs for consumer technology.

Much of this early industrial growth was built around an arrangement known as “front shop, back factory,” wherein Hong Kong based firms handled financing and facilitated access to international markets, while businesses across the border in Guangdong took on much of the manufacturing. Riding this industrial boom, Shenzhen transformed from a small border town into one of China’s premier manufacturing and technology centers.

By the 2010s, Beijing had begun making plans to more closely integrate the area into a single regional economic strategy. The Greater Bay Area development plan, announced in 2019, set out to link nine mainland cities with Hong Kong and Macao, with the goal of creating an internationally competitive “world-class city cluster.” Though the varying monikers of “megacity” and “megapolis” are often used in international media to describe the GBA, the project is not a single city, but rather a sprawling network of cities with distinct economies and local governments.

Each city in the plan has its own role. Hong Kong remains the region’s financial and international trade center, while Macao is positioned as a tourism hub. Guangzhou, the provincial capital, brings its strengths in commerce and scientific research, while Shenzhen is expected to lead in technological innovation and venture capital. Smaller cities like Dongguan and Foshan, meanwhile, remain important manufacturing centers, with dense networks of suppliers and factories supporting the region’s industrial base.

Binding this network together requires the construction of massive physical infrastructure projects, which officials call “hard connectivity.” Projects like the Guangzhou–Shenzhen–Hong Kong Express Rail Link have accelerated travel speed, cutting the train ride between Hong Kong’s West Kowloon station and Shenzhen’s Futian station to just 14 minutes. The long-term goal is to make it possible to travel between each of the region’s major cities within an hour.

However, many researchers note that the GBA is still lagging behind on “soft connectivity,” or legal integration. Though ostensibly a unified market, the GBA lacks any single government or legislature able to enact common laws across all 11 jurisdictions – Hong Kong and Macao retain their own legal systems as special administrative regions, while the mainland cities operate under Chinese law. For example, something as simple as transferring personal data between a company in Shenzhen and one in Hong Kong can involve navigating two separate legal codes on privacy. And while Beijing has laid out a broad strategy, local governments in the region still actively compete with one another for capital and talent.

Beijing’s plans for greater integration have also aroused political concerns in Hong Kong, where some residents worry that closer ties with the mainland could gradually erode the city’s autonomy. During the unveiling of the plan in 2019, former Hong Kong legislator Alvin Yeung warned that being “planned” in this way only made people worry that Hong Kong’s distinctive status might be weakened. A 2025 survey by the Chinese University of Hong Kong found that only 39.4 percent of respondents viewed the GBA as an opportunity for Hong Kong, while 21.5 percent disagreed and 32.2 percent remained undecided. Those concerns persist even as Hong Kong’s newly released First Five-Year Plan commits the city to further integrating with the mainland.

Ultimately, Beijing wants this regional network to help China move beyond low cost manufacturing, and become a leader in the technologies it currently imports or relies on foreign companies to develop. China’s 15th Five Year Plan places renewed emphasis on technological self sufficiency, with the aim of strengthening domestic capabilities in areas like semiconductors, artificial intelligence, robotics, and biotechnology. With the GBA, Beijing hopes to create an innovation powerhouse that can rival other major technology hubs like the San Francisco Bay Area.

The choice of Shenzhen as the host city for this year’s APEC is in itself, an important part of Beijing’s effort to tell the story of “the Chinese miracle.” When Xi Jinping announced Shenzhen as the host at the APEC handover ceremony in November 2025, he told how the city had grown “from a backward fishing village into a modern metropolis,” calling it “a miracle created by the Chinese people in world-development history.” This narrative is familiar to Shenzhen, which has become one of the most visible symbols of China’s economic transformation.

In an interview with Chinese media, Hong Kong representative to APEC’s Business Advisory Council Yang Min-de said that “an increasingly successful and efficiently coordinated Greater Bay Area cluster can not only support China’s high-quality development, but also offer an example for APEC economies to learn from.” The summit gives Beijing an opportunity to present a distinctly Chinese model of development – of which Shenzhen and the Greater Bay Area have become so emblematic. By showcasing the region on the world stage, Beijing is making a case for its own approach to development and seeks to position China not only as an economic power, but as a source of leadership for the region’s future.
